== Biography ==

'''Adam de Glasgeu''' (fl. undated; probably fourteenth century) was a burgess
of Berwick-upon-Tweed who held ten acres of arable land called Hiddeslaw in
the tenement of Bondington outside Berwick.

=== Charter to Melrose Abbey ===

Adam is known from an undated charter printed in the appendix to the
''Liber Sancte Marie de Melros''. It begins:

<blockquote>
''Sciant presentes et futuri quod ego Adam de Glasgeu, burgensis burgi
Berwici super Twedam ...''
</blockquote>

That is:

<blockquote>
Let all present and future know that I, Adam de Glasgeu, burgess of the
burgh of Berwick-upon-Tweed ...
</blockquote>

Adam granted to Melrose Abbey ten acres of arable land called Hiddeslaw,
situated in the tenement of Bondington, with free entry and exit and its
ancient boundaries.<ref name="MelroseApp25">Cosmo Innes, ed.,
''Liber Sancte Marie de Melros: Munimenta Vetustiora Monasterii
Cisterciensis de Melros'', vol. 2 (Edinburgh, 1837), Appendix no. 25,
p. 688.</ref>

The land was bounded:

* towards the east by land of the nuns of Berwick and the house of
  St Mary Magdalene;
* towards the north by land of the abbot and convent of Kelso and by
  land of the Berwick nuns; and
* towards the south by the royal highway leading from the house of
  St Mary Magdalene to the village of Bondington.

No western boundary is preserved in the printed copy.

The grant was made in pure and perpetual alms. Melrose was to hold the
land of Adam and his heirs while performing the customary services owed
to the chief lords of the fee. Adam and his heirs warranted the land to
the monks against all people. This establishes that Adam possessed an
alienable heritable interest in the property, but the superior lord or
lords are not identified.

=== Date and Source Transmission ===

Adam's charter contains no date. The ''Dedications to Saints in Medieval
Scotland'' database classifies it as possibly fourteenth century but gives
no narrower date.<ref name="DSSAdam">''Dedications to Saints in Medieval
Scotland'', document DO/JD/2961, “Possible 14th c. in date”.</ref>

Innes labelled his source “Regist. recent.” rather than “Orig.” The text
therefore survives through a later Melrose register, not through a known
original charter. The surviving copy ends with an abbreviation for
“witnesses”, but no witness names are preserved. A date such as
c. 1280–1294 cannot presently be justified.

The safest description is therefore “undated, probably fourteenth
century”. An early-fourteenth-century date is possible, but remains
unproved.

=== Bondington Context ===

Kelso Abbey held a substantial estate at Bondington. In 1266 it leased
its whole ploughgate there, with buildings and crofts, to Thomas Batail,
burgess of Berwick. A further Kelso deed dated 1307 describes a cottage
and garden in the village of Bondington adjoining Kelso land and a royal
road.<ref name="KelsoBondington">Cosmo Innes, ed., ''Liber S. Marie de
Calchou'', vol. 1 (Edinburgh, 1846), nos. 42 and 48, pp. 35, 40–41.</ref>

These records confirm the kind of monastic and burgess landholding
landscape described in Adam's charter, but they do not date his deed.

=== Name and Family ===

Adam's designation ''de Glasgeu'' is a locative byname meaning “of” or
“from Glasgow”. This single occurrence does not establish that the name
was hereditary.

The reference to Adam's heirs is standard warranty language. It does not
name a wife, child or other relative, and no heir is known to have used
the Glasgow name.

No evidence has been found connecting Adam with John de Glasgu, the
Duffield family, later Glasgow families of the Borders, or any modern
Y-DNA lineage.

Adam was not the first securely dated bearer of the designation in a
secular context. Alexander de Glasgow, an escheator, appears in a Scottish
Exchequer account rendered in 1289.<ref name="AlexanderGlasgow">George
Burnett, ed., ''The Exchequer Rolls of Scotland'', vol. 1 (Edinburgh,
1878), p. 47.</ref>

=== Research Status ===

Adam is presently known from one record. His occupation, parentage,
marriage, children, precise date and later fate are unknown.

'''Records:''' 1.

=== Possible identity with Adam called Moses of Bondington ===

A separate Bondington title records Nicholas called Moses as the son and
heir of the late Adam called Moses of Bondington. Nicholas had earlier
styled himself:

<blockquote>
''Nicholaus dictus Moyses de Bondyngton''
</blockquote>

The coexistence of ''dictus Moyses'' and ''de Bondyngton'' demonstrates
that a personal or familial byname and a locative could be used together.
The names alone therefore do not exclude the possibility that Adam called
Moses was elsewhere styled Adam ''de Glasgeu'', particularly if
''de Glasgeu'' denoted his origin while ''Moyses'' was his family
byname.<ref name="NicholasMoyses1307">Cosmo Innes, ed.,
''Liber S. Marie de Calchou'', vol. 1 (Edinburgh, 1846), no. 42,
pp. 35–36.</ref>

The property evidence is also compatible. Nicholas held land at
Bondington adjoining Kelso Abbey property and a royal road. Adam de
Glasgeu's Hiddeslaw acres likewise adjoined Kelso property and the royal
road leading from St Mary Magdalene's house to Bondington. The parcels
are not demonstrably identical, but they lay within the same local
landholding landscape.

The identification remains unproved. No record calls Adam
''de Glasgeu dictus Moyses'', no charter describes Nicholas as the son
of Adam de Glasgeu, and Hiddeslaw has not been identified within the land
which Nicholas inherited and later resigned to Robert I.

Adam de Glasgeu and Adam called Moses should therefore remain separate
working identities. Possible identity may be recorded as a research
hypothesis but should not be used to attach Nicholas as Adam de
Glasgeu's son.

Even if the men were identical, Nicholas is recorded under the inherited
byname ''Moyses'', not ''de Glasgu''. The identification would therefore
not by itself prove hereditary transmission of the Glasgow designation.
